Before diving into the individual meanings, here is the golden key that unlocks all of them: heave always involves effort, force, and significant movement. Whatever you are doing when you "heave," something is being pushed, pulled, lifted, thrown, or physically strained — and it never feels light or easy. Keep that in mind, and all the meanings will click into place naturally.

1. To lift or move something heavy with great physical effort

This is the most fundamental meaning. When you heave something, you are not casually picking it up — you are working hard against weight and resistance to move it.

  • She heaved the suitcase onto the overhead shelf.
  • The workers heaved the fallen tree off the road.

Notice: you would never say you "heaved" a pen or a piece of paper. You heave things that are heavy, awkward, or resistant. The word itself communicates the struggle.

2. To throw something with force (especially something heavy)

When you heave something through the air, you throw it powerfully — either because it is heavy, or because you are putting your whole body's effort behind it.

  • He heaved a rock into the river.
  • She heaved her bag across the room in frustration.

The difference between "throw" and "heave" is important: throwing can be quick, light, and effortless. Heaving always implies weight, force, or muscular strain. A baseball pitcher throws the ball. A person in anger heaves a chair.

3. To rise and fall in a slow, powerful, repeated rhythm

This is where the word becomes more expressive and visual. Something "heaves" when it moves up and down in large, rolling, repetitive waves of motion.

  • The sea heaves — the ocean rises and falls in great swells.
  • Your chest heaves — your chest rises and falls rapidly and visibly, usually after sprinting, sobbing, or in a moment of intense emotion.
  • The ground heaved — the earth shifted violently upward, as in an earthquake or an explosion underground.

The crucial detail here is that a heaving motion is not small or quick. It is large, powerful, and sustained. A heaving ocean is not choppy — it is rolling in massive, muscular waves. A heaving chest is not breathing quietly — it is visibly, dramatically working.

4. To retch — to make the physical movements of vomiting

When your stomach "heaves," your body is performing the muscular convulsions of trying to vomit, whether or not anything actually comes out. When nothing comes out, this is called dry heaving.

  • The stench from the garbage was so overwhelming, it made his stomach heave.
  • She was dry heaving by the side of the road after the race.

This meaning connects directly to meaning #3: the stomach is literally rising and falling in violent, involuntary spasms. The word is the same because the motion is the same — just inside the body instead of on the ocean.

5. To pull hard — especially on ropes or equipment

In sailing and heavy physical work, "heave" means to pull something with great, sustained force.

  • "Heave on that rope!" — Pull it with everything you have!
  • The sailors heaved the anchor chain up from the water.

This is where the famous exclamation "Heave-ho!" comes from. It was the rhythmic chant sailors called out to coordinate their collective pulling — a verbal beat to synchronize their effort, like a work song. Today, "heave-ho" has also become a casual expression for firing or dismissing someone: "The company gave him the old heave-ho" means he was let go.
The Most Common Phrases You Will Encounter

"Heave a sigh" — to let out a deep, heavy breath. "She heaved a sigh of relief when the exam was over." Notice the connection to meaning #3: even a sigh involves the chest rising and falling with effort.

"Heave into sight" / "heave into view" — to gradually come into visibility, the way a ship slowly appears on the horizon. "The mountain finally heaved into view after hours of driving through fog." The image is of something large and heavy slowly rising up into your line of sight.

"Heave to" — a nautical command or action meaning to bring a ship to a near-stop by adjusting the sails against each other so they cancel out. In general use, it simply means "stop" or "hold your position."

"Heave" has two past tense forms, and both are correct — but they are used in different contexts:

Heaved is the standard, everyday past tense used by almost everyone in almost every situation. "She heaved the box onto the shelf." This is always safe and correct.

Hove is an older, traditional past tense used primarily in nautical (sailing) language and in older literature. "The ship hove into sight." You may encounter "hove" in classic novels or sailing texts, but you will rarely hear it in everyday speech. Stick with "heaved" unless you are writing about ships in a historical or literary context.
The Full Picture in One Paragraph

"Heave" is the verb of effort. It covers every kind of forceful, strenuous physical movement — lifting a heavy object, throwing something with power, the rhythmic rise and fall of the sea or a chest, the convulsions of a sick stomach, and the hard pull of a sailor on a rope. Whatever you heave, whatever heaves, there is always weight, strain, and motion behind it. If something is light and easy, it does not heave. If it is heavy, powerful, rhythmic, or violent — that is when heave is exactly the right word.
